"# Quoting speech

Read this before putting quotation marks around anything somebody said. It applies to interview transcripts, recorded remarks, meeting notes, and any other material where the words are a person's rather than a document's.

Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.

When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.

## What may be repaired

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

## What stays outside this

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved."

5	## Brief
6	
7	Write a journalistic customer case for operations managers at small housing companies. The publisher is the supplier, Svale Systems. The customer, Elm Quay Housing, should remain the acting party. 9	## Material
10	
11	Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats. In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings. Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately. The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information. It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available.
12	
13	The maintenance team designed its categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents. Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions. The trial lasted eight weeks. # Source-comparison report 2

Draft: scratch/write-run.1bsQps/draft.md
Source: work/source.md (brief and material)
Language: en_US. The source is in English too, so no quotation is translated. The three quotations are checked for fidelity only; there are no translation findings.

## Claim accounting

Each item gives the draft passage (D), the source passage (S) in the source's words, and what differs.

### Title
1. D: "Elm Quay's maintenance shifts trial a shared log"
   S: "its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings." / "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information."
   Difference: the subject has changed from the team to "shifts". The source says the team decided on and ran the trial. Shifts appear only as the aim of the trial ("wanted ... to see"). -> Finding F1.

### Standfirst
2. D: "For eight weeks in two of its buildings, Elm Quay Housing entered repair reports into a log from Svale Systems."
   S: "The trial lasted eight weeks." / "trial a shared repair log in two buildings" / "31 repair reports were entered" / "We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports" (Lind) / "Svale configured the log".
   Difference: the source's passive "were entered" becomes Elm Quay as the agent. Lind's "we ... entering the first reports" supports that. Supported.
3. D: "This account follows how the maintenance team set it up, what its internal figures do and do not show, and what its supervisor would do differently."
   S: "The maintenance team designed its categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents." / "Elm Quay's internal trial note" / "I would set that time aside before the next building starts." / "I would leave an extra week for preparation."
   Difference: "set it up" covers the team's own actions: the decision, the categories and keeping telephone reporting open. The body credits the configuration to Svale. Supported.

### Byline
4. D: "By Thomas". This comes from the invocation, so there is no finding.

### Opening paragraph
5. D: "Telephone repair reports and emails used to be stored separately at Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 flats."
   S: "Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats." / "Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately."
   Difference: none of substance. Supported.
6. D: "In September 2025 its maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings."
   S: "In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings."
   Difference: none. Supported.
7. D: "An internal trial note and the maintenance supervisor's own assessment record how it went."
   S: "Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025" / "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment."
   Difference: none of substance. Supported.

### "## Why Elm Quay chose a shared log"
8. Heading. S: "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information." The reason is carried by Lind's first quotation below. Supported.
9. D: "Before settling on Svale Systems as its supplier, the team tested whether the log could show the status of each repair."
   S: "It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available."
   Difference: "settling on" means deciding on. The draft does not claim that any other supplier was compared. Supported.
10. D: "Maya Lind, the maintenance supervisor, was interviewed by email."
    S: "Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind" / "All interviews occurred by email".
    Supported.
11. D (quotation): "We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done," she says. "The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log."
    S: "We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log."
    Difference: none; the quotation is verbatim. Pronoun "she": third person, singular, feminine natural gender. The feminine gender is supported by S: "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment." The present-tense "says" is attribution convention; the draft already states that the interview was by email.

### "## Six staff learn the log in two sessions"
12. Heading. D: "Six staff learn the log in two sessions"
    S: "Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions."
    Difference: "trained" (an activity by Svale) has become "learn" (an outcome for the staff). -> Finding F2.
13. D: "Residents could still report repairs by telephone."
    S: "kept telephone reporting open for residents."
    Difference: the agent (the maintenance team) is omitted, but nothing is misattributed. Supported.
14. D: "Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions, and the trial ran for eight weeks."
    S: "Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions. The trial lasted eight weeks."
    Supported. The supplier is narrated in the third person.
15. D (quotation): "We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports," Lind says of the preparation. "I would set that time aside before the next building starts."
    S: "We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts."
    Difference: the quotation is verbatim. The frame "of the preparation" rests on the quotation itself ("set that time aside before the next building starts") and on quotation 3 ("an extra week for preparation"). Supported.

### "## The trial note does not credit the software"
16. Heading. D: "The trial note does not credit the software"
    S: "the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
    Difference: the scope has widened, from "the difference" (in median time to assignment) to the software in general. -> Finding F3.
17. D: "Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, counts 31 repair reports entered, excluding emergencies and work ordered before the trial began."
    S: "Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial."
    Difference: the date is given in US format, and the exclusions are kept. Supported.
18. D: "Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial, against three in the preceding eight weeks."
    S: "Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period."
    Difference: none. The measure stays assignment time, not completion time. Supported.
19. D: "The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
    S: "The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
    Supported. No causal claim is made.
20. D: "Costs, resident satisfaction and completion times were not measured."
    S: "There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements."
    Difference: "there are no measurements" becomes "were not measured". In ordinary reading these say the same thing. Supported.

### "## Lind looks back on the eight weeks"
21. D (quotation): "I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation," Lind says.
    S: the same words.
    Verbatim. The qualification survives.
22. D: "She stops short of recommending Svale to every housing company."
    S: "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company."
    Difference: "stops short of" implies that Lind moved partway towards a recommendation of Svale. The source only records that she did not recommend Svale to every housing company. -> Finding F4. Pronoun "she": as in item 11, supported.
23. D: "The trial has not yet been extended beyond the two buildings; the team will decide after checking how its categories work for larger repairs."
    S: "The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs." / "The maintenance team designed its categories".
    Difference: "beyond the two buildings" is narrower than "has not yet expanded", but the source's statement entails it. Lind's "before the next building starts" also supports reading expansion as more buildings. "its categories" is supported. Supported.

### "## Read the checklist before a trial of your own"
24. Heading and D: "Operations managers weighing a shared log can start with the [implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist), a document to read before planning a trial."
    S (brief): "The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read, not a consultation booking or a product trial."
    Difference: the link text and description match the destination: an implementation checklist and a document to read. "before planning a trial" is advice from the author and the publisher, not a claim about what the checklist contains. Supported.
25. D: "The eight weeks left Elm Quay with figures its own note does not credit to the software and a qualified assessment from its supervisor."
    S: "the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software." / "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment."
    Difference: "figures ... does not credit" refers to the before-and-after comparison, which is the difference the note does not attribute. This is a reasonable summary. Supported.

### Forbidden inferences (brief)
- No claim that the software caused the shorter assignment time, saved money or pleased residents, and no rescue framing. Assignment time is never turned into completion time.
- The customer's reservation survives in items 21 and 22. Item 22 should still be repaired (F4).

## Findings (source support)

**F1. Title: the subject has changed from the team to the shifts.**
- Draft: "Elm Quay's maintenance shifts trial a shared log"
- Source: "its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log"; "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information."
- In the source, the team ran the trial. The shifts appear only as its aim: the team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information.
- Concrete case: the six trained staff all worked morning shifts, and evening-shift staff took no part in the trial. The material does not exclude this. Lind says the team "wanted" the evening shift to see the morning shift's work, not that both shifts used the log. In that case the source holds and the title fails.
- Repair: "Elm Quay's maintenance team trials a shared log".

**F2. Section heading: "trained" has become "learn".**
- Draft: "Six staff learn the log in two sessions"
- Source: "Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions."
- The source reports that training was given, not what the staff learned.
- Concrete case: six staff attended two training sessions but had not yet mastered the log. This is compatible with the material, and nothing supplied excludes it. In that case the source holds and the heading fails.
- Repair: "Six staff trained in two sessions".

**F3. Section heading: "does not credit the software" is wider than the source.**
- Draft: "The trial note does not credit the software"
- Source: "the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
- The source limits the non-attribution to the difference in median time to assignment. The heading extends it to the software in general.
- Concrete case: the note credits the log with making repair status visible across shifts, while explicitly not attributing the change in assignment time to it. Nothing supplied excludes this, because the material does not give the note's full contents. In that case the source holds and the heading fails.
- Repair: "The trial note does not credit the software with the difference", or "The trial note does not attribute the shorter assignment time to the software".

**F4. Lind's reservation: "stops short of" adds a stance.**
- Draft: "She stops short of recommending Svale to every housing company."
- Source: "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company."
- "Stops short of" suggests that Lind went some way towards recommending Svale. The source records only that she did not recommend it to every housing company. Her quotations endorse repeating the trial and one view of the reports; they do not recommend Svale as such.
- Concrete case: Lind made no recommendation of Svale to anyone. This is compatible with the material: the only statements are that she did not recommend Svale to every company, and her quotations, none of which recommend Svale. In that case the source holds, but the draft misstates her stance.
- Repair: "She did not recommend Svale to every housing company."

## Translation findings
None. No quotation is translated, and all three quotations are verbatim.

## Outside this comparison (noted, not findings)
The brief says the case is "supplier-published material; it is not independent journalism". The draft contains no disclosure of this. It also makes no claim to be independent, so this is an editorial and brief-compliance matter, not a source-support defect.

## Completion status
Complete. Every factual and attributed claim, heading, quotation and pronoun in the draft has been accounted for against the source.

Unresolved findings: F1, F2, F3 and F4. All four are source-support findings, and each has the smallest supported repair proposed above. There are no translation findings.
